strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically important problem (multi-subject, reference-image-conditioned video generation), and the proposed hierarchical attention decomposition (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal) is a sensible and clearly motivated alternative to naive token concatenation in MMDiT.

Using a pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as a joint text/visual encoder to enrich conditioning semantics is a reasonable design choice, and the ablation in Table 2 suggests it improves text-video alignment (49.55% vs 42.17%).

The data curation pipeline (Fig. 3, Appendix C) using VLMs and image-editing models to build subject-decomposed reference data, plus the dataset statistics, provides useful resources for the community.
The paper is generally well written and organized, the method section is readable, and detailed architecture configurations are provided in Appendix B/Table 3.
The idea of applying online RL (Flow-GRPO) with task-specific verifiable rewards for subject-consistent video generation is a natural but underexplored direction.
weaknesses: Serious concerns about the reliability of the reported numbers. In Table 1, the results of the proposed models are suspiciously round (42.50%, 38.00%, 60.50%, 64.00%, 67.00%, 45.00%, 71.00%, 73.00%) while all baselines have three-decimal values, which is highly atypical of actual benchmark runs and raises questions about whether these results were genuinely measured.

Inconsistencies between tables undermine the evidence: Table 2 lists the 'Full Model' with Total Score 54.33% and FaceSim 58.12%, which exactly matches 'Ours-1.3B' in Table 1, yet Table 2 reports metrics ('Text-Video Align', 'Video Quality') that are not part of the OpenS2V-Nexus protocol used in Table 1, and the protocol for Table 2 is not defined. It is unclear which model (1.3B or 14B) the ablations refer to.

The online RL stage is one of three headline contributions, but there is NO quantitative ablation for it: it is evaluated only qualitatively in Figure 5. Given the authors' own claim that RL 'drives the overall training objective into RLVR' and mitigates reward hacking, quantitative evidence (e.g., 'w/o RL' rows, reward curves, training stability, signs of reward hacking) is essential and missing.

Appendix B.2 ('Details of Reward Calculation') is an empty placeholder: the reward functions R_qual and R_id, their implementations (which face/identity model?), and the weights lambda are never specified. This makes the RL phase non-reproducible and the claim of 'verifiable rewards' unverifiable.

Novelty is limited: the hierarchical attention is a straightforward sequence of self-attention stages, VLM-as-text-encoder has been explored (e.g., CINEMA uses MLLM-based guidance), and Flow-GRPO is applied essentially as-is with a composite reward. The contribution is largely an engineering combination of existing components.

No human evaluation or user study is provided anywhere; all conclusions rest on automated metrics of questionable validity (e.g., NaturalScore is a raw MLLM-judged score). Qualitative comparisons in Figure 4 are too dense and low-resolution to substantiate claims of 'superior visual quality' and identity preservation.

Notation and presentation errors: Eq. (3) has undefined/misformatted terms, typos ('determinsitic', 'down-sample ration'), and a clearly wrong citation (DPO attributed to Gao et al., 2025, which is the Seedream report). The '14B' variant is claimed in Table 1 but the implementation details describe a single training run at 480p without clarifying the 14B configuration or its training.

Reproducibility promises are unmet at review time: no code, models, or data released; the evaluation prompt set (180 subject-text pairs) and Total Score weighting are only partially described, so the headline SOTA claim cannot be independently verified.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and timely problem: multi-subject identity-preserving video generation from a text prompt plus reference images, where existing concatenation-based approaches (Phantom, SkyReels-A2, CINEMA) indeed struggle with subject–prompt conflicts.

The proposed three-level (intra-subject / inter-subject / cross-modal) attention decomposition is a reasonable and clearly motivated alternative to flat token concatenation, and the ablation in Table 2 (FaceSim dropping from 58.12% to 51.34% without it) supports its benefit.

The data-curation pipeline (VLM-based filtering/captioning, subject decomposition via Grounded-SAM + SAM, and reference-image synthesis with an in-context image editing model) is described in reasonable detail, and the dataset statistics (Appendix C.1) and comparison of reference-construction strategies (Fig. 9, Appendix C.2) add value to the community.
The evaluation follows an established public protocol (OpenS2V-Nexus, 180 subject-text pairs) with standard metrics, and comparisons cover both open-source and proprietary systems.
The authors promise code, models, and data release, and include an LLM-usage declaration.
weaknesses: Credibility of the quantitative results is a serious concern. In Table 1, essentially all scores for 'Ours-1.3B' and 'Ours-14B' are suspiciously round (38.00%, 40.00%, 42.50%, 58.12%->58.12% is the only exception; 60.50%, 64.00%, 67.00%, 43.00%, 45.00%, 71.00%, 73.00%), while every baseline is reported to two decimals. This pattern strongly suggests post-hoc rounding or imprecise reporting and undermines confidence in the headline claims of state-of-the-art performance.

Internal inconsistencies: the ablation 'ID-Composer (Full Model)' in Table 2 (FaceSim 58.12%, Total 54.33%) exactly matches 'Ours-1.3B (Base Model)' in Table 1, yet the architecture details (Appendix B.1) describe a 14B DiT. It is unclear whether ablations were run on the 1.3B or 14B model, and whether the flagship 14B results were ever ablated. Additionally, training a 14B model for 30,000 iterations on only 16 H20 GPUs at 480p (Sec. 4.1) appears implausible and contradicts the stated initialization from Wan-Video-1.3B.

Overclaiming contradicted by the paper's own tables: Sec. 4.2 claims 'state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation metrics,' but Ours-1.3B scores lower than Phantom-1.3B on Aesthetics (42.50% vs 46.67%), lower than VACE-1.3B (48.24%), and its GmeScore (64.00%) trails VACE-1.3B, Phantom-1.3B, Phantom-14B, and SkyReels-A2. The claimed superiority does not hold 'across all metrics.'

The RL contribution is not quantitatively validated. Section 3.3 and Eq. (5) motivate the online RL phase as a core contribution, but there is no ablation with/without RL in Table 2; only a qualitative Figure 5 is provided. Appendix B.2 ('Details of Reward Calculation') is essentially empty—the reward components Rqual and Rid, the verifiable-reward design, and the weights lambda_qual/lambda_id are never specified, making the RLVR claim unverifiable and unreproducible.

Limited technical novelty. The hierarchical attention is a staged application of self-attention over partitioned token sets—closely related to existing local-global attention designs the authors themselves cite (Wang et al. 2025a; Lin et al. 2025). Using a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as text/conditioning encoder follows prior MLLM-guided generation work, including CINEMA (Deng et al., 2025b), which the paper cites as closest related work; the delta over CINEMA is not clearly articulated. Flow-GRPO is applied essentially off-the-shelf with a new reward.

Method description has gaps and inconsistencies: Sec. 3.2.1 first states the prompt is encoded by 'a pretrained text encoder' and then that VLM tokens 'replace' these embeddings; the dual T5+Qwen2.5-VL setup only appears in Sec. 4.1. FaceSim, a headline metric, is never defined (unlike NexusScore/NaturalScore/GmeScore in Appendix D). The advantage operator in Eq. (3) mixes notation ({r1..rn} vs. G and oi).

Evaluation breadth is thin: 180 prompts from a single benchmark, no human study, no variance/confidence reporting, and no evaluation of multi-subject identity confusion (e.g., attribute binding/subject swapping), which is the central failure mode motivating the paper.
Reproducibility is currently insufficient: code/models are only 'will be released,' the dataset curation prompts and reward details are missing, and the numbers themselves are unreliable as reported.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely problem — multi-subject, subject-driven video generation — and achieves the best reported Total Score on the public OpenS2V-Nexus benchmark (57.05% for the 14B variant vs. 54.46% for Kling 1.6 and 52.87% for VACE-14B), with clear gains on the identity-related metric FaceSim (60.50% vs. 55.09% for the next best open-source model).

The hierarchical identity-preserving attention (intra-subject -> inter-subject -> cross-modal) is a sensible and clearly motivated response to the identified weakness of prior methods that simply concatenate all subject and text tokens; the ablation (FaceSim drops from 58.12% to 51.34% without it) provides direct evidence for its benefit.

The paper is honest about the need to go beyond the diffusion loss and introduces an online RL phase (Flow-GRPO/GRPO) with task-specific rewards for subject-consistent video generation, an application area where online RL has indeed been underexplored.

A new data-curation pipeline combining VLM-based filtering/captioning with image-editing-based subject decomposition is described, with dataset statistics (Appendix C) and a comparison of reference-image construction strategies (Fig. 9); the 'w/o Curated Data' ablation shows measurable gains across metrics.

Both 1.3B and 14B variants are trained and evaluated, allowing scaling comparisons against Phantom and VACE at matched sizes; the authors commit to releasing code, models, and the training data, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The reinforcement learning contribution, presented as one of the three pillars of the paper, is severely under-documented. Section B.2 ('Details of Reward Calculation') is an empty heading with no content. The reward functions R_qual and R_id are never defined (Eq. 5 only states a weighted sum), the weights lambda_qual/lambda_id, the number of rollouts, group size, RL iterations, or any hyperparameters are unspecified, and there is no quantitative RL ablation: the effect of online RL is shown only via qualitative frames in Fig. 5, and it is absent from Table 2. As written, the RL claim is essentially unverifiable.

Novelty is largely incremental. The hierarchical attention is a direct extension of existing local-global attention designs (Wang et al., 2025a; Lin et al., 2025) applied to subject tokens; using a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as a multimodal encoder for subject-driven video generation closely mirrors CINEMA (Deng et al., 2025b), which the paper cites but does not quantitatively compare against; and the RL stage is a straightforward application of Flow-GRPO with task-specific rewards. The paper's positioning against CINEMA, Concat-ID, and UniVideo — its closest relatives — is qualitative only.

Some reported numbers raise credibility concerns. The Ours-14B row in Table 1 consists almost entirely of round values (45.00%, 40.00%, 60.50%, 67.00%, 45.00%, 73.00%), unlike every other row; the Total Score weighting scheme is not specified despite the appendix claiming 'further details are provided in Appendix D' (only three metric definitions are given, and the weights are not listed). These should be corrected with exact values.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: Section B.1 states the DiT is 'a substantial 14B parameter transformer' while Table 3 lists 1.3B/14B; the VLM is described both as a text-encoder replacement for f_txt (Sec. 3.2.1) and as encoding subject images (B.1); the abstract claims the objective is driven 'into RLVR' but the rewards are learned/heuristic preference-style metrics rather than clearly verifiable ones. Typos ('determinsitic', 'down-sample ration') and an awkwardly rendered Fig. 4 further suggest a rushed manuscript.

Evaluation breadth is limited: metrics are entirely automated (CLIP-style similarity, MLLM-judged scores); FaceSim only measures facial identity, leaving non-face subject fidelity (objects, clothing) under-measured; there is no human evaluation or user study; and comparisons with proprietary systems are qualitative only. The benchmark is also the same one used to build the training data source (OpenS2V-Nexus), which raises a potential train/test leakage concern that is not discussed.

Ablations are conducted only on the 1.3B base model (Table 2 matches the Ours-1.3B row), so it is unclear whether component contributions hold at 14B; the ablation table also lacks the RL condition despite RL being a headline contribution.

strengths: The paper presents a complete, well-engineered system (hierarchical identity-preserving attention + VLM-based semantic grounding + GRPO-style online RL) that achieves state-of-the-art total score (57.05% for the 14B model) on the OpenS2V-Nexus benchmark, outperforming Phantom-14B, SkyReels-A2, and VACE-14B.

The experimental support is unusually thorough for a systems paper: ablations on each attention stage (Table S.5), the VLM encoder, curated data, RL algorithm comparison against offline DPO (Table 3), reward-component ablations, a gamma sensitivity study for the fidelity reward (Table S.7), and a human preference study (30 participants, 200 questionnaires) that partially addresses circularity concerns about automated metrics.

The reward-hacking analysis is honest and informative: removing the Natural reward increases FaceSim/Aesthetics but degrades Q-Align, which the authors correctly interpret as metric over-optimization and use to justify the multi-faceted reward design.

The data curation pipeline is well documented (Table S.8, Figures S.8/S.12), including a comparison of reference-image construction strategies (naive augmentation vs. Flux-Kontext vs. GPT-4o vs. Nano Banana), and the evaluation set is stated to be held out and disjoint from training data.

The online RL application to multi-subject subject-consistent video generation is a relatively under-explored combination, and the stochastic-sampling formulation for flow-matching policy optimization (Eq. 4) is described concretely enough to be reproducible in spirit.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the individual components are largely assembled from existing work — gated cross-attention (Flamingo-style) for the hierarchical attention, VLM conditioning already explored by CINEMA [6], and GRPO for diffusion already established by Flow-GRPO/Dance-GRPO [28, 62]. The claimed first ('no prior open-source work has integrated a VLM as the core reasoning engine within Wan-Video') is a weak, architecture-specific novelty claim.

Overclaiming relative to the evidence: the text asserts state-of-the-art performance 'across all evaluation metrics,' yet Table 1 shows the RL stage degrades GmeScore (64.06% to 62.20%) and NaturalScore (71.09% to 71.09% -> 69.15%), and the margin over the strongest proprietary baseline (Kling 1.6, 54.46%) on Total Score is modest for the 1.3B model (55.16%).

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: the ablation discussion claims the 'w/o VLM Encoder' variant shows 'a marked decrease in Text-Video Alignment,' but Table 2 reports no alignment metric (only Q-Align, which is a perceptual quality score); there is a broken cross-reference ('As shown in Tab. ??') on page 8; and the appendix promises a 'D.1 Evaluation on Multi-Subject Scenarios' section whose content is absent. The 14B model's FaceSim (60.71%) being lower than the 1.3B RL model (66.10%) is not explained.

Main-paper method description is thin on the hierarchical attention mechanism — the actual gated inter-subject formulation (Eq. S.10) and the choice of injecting the block only in the first 20 layers are relegated to the appendix, making the central contribution hard to assess in the main text.

The GRPO objective (Eq. 3) contains notational errors (subscript 'o_i,t', malformed KL term, undefined t-index over a continuous-time diffusion trajectory), suggesting the formulation was adapted from LLM RL notation without careful verification.

Evaluation relies partly on metrics derived from the authors' own ecosystem (NexusScore, NaturalScore from OpenS2V-Nexus, which the authors also build the training data upon [68]), and the human study protocol (30 raters, forced choice among five models) is under-specified regarding statistical testing.

Contradictory terminology and copy-editing issues ('copy-plate' vs 'copy-paste' artifacts, determinsitic, sentence beginning 'unlike conventional text encoders') indicate the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

strengths: Comprehensive system-level treatment of multi-subject video generation: the paper combines hierarchical identity attention, VLM-based semantic conditioning, online GRPO post-training, and a curated data pipeline, with ablations for each component (Tables 2, 3, S.5, S.7).

Results on the OpenS2V-Nexus protocol show meaningful quantitative gains over strong open-source baselines (e.g., FaceSim 66.10% vs. Phantom-14B 51.48%), supported by a human preference study (Fig. S.13) and qualitative comparisons against proprietary systems.

The reward-hacking analysis (removing the Natural reward increases FaceSim/Aesthetics but degrades Q-Align) and the gamma ablation for average vs. minimum face identity are thoughtful experimental design choices.
The supplementary material provides substantial implementation detail (architecture table, GRPO hyperparameters, dataset composition), which supports reproducibility relative to many system papers.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: all three components are adaptations of existing work — attention-based subject injection closely follows Phantom/CINEMA/Concat-ID, VLM-guided conditioning follows CINEMA, and the RL stage is a direct application of Flow-GRPO. The claim of 'pioneering online RL for multi-subject video generation' is contradicted by the authors' own citation of Identity-GRPO [33], which already applies GRPO to identity-preserving video generation.

Overstated claims contradicted by the paper's own results: Sec. 4.2 claims state-of-the-art 'across all evaluation metrics,' yet Ours-14B (67.49%) loses to VACE-14B (73.27%) on GmeScore, and the 1.3B RL model drops GmeScore from 64.06% to 62.20% and NaturalScore from 71.09% to 69.15%. The claimed trade-off between identity and alignment is not analyzed or resolved.

Circularity in evaluation: two of the four primary metrics (NexusScore, NaturalScore) come from the authors' own benchmark (OpenS2V-Nexus [68]) and appear directly as reward terms (Rsubject, Rnat) in training. Optimizing against metrics that are also the headline evaluation criteria weakens the evidential value of the reported gains; the human study partially mitigates this but its protocol (200 questionnaires, 30 participants) is under-specified (e.g., no details on rating procedure or inter-annotator agreement).

Presentation is not ready for publication: the GRPO objective (Eq. 3) is a pasted fragment ending mid-sentence with a dangling 'the relative quality...' clause; Eq. 4 begins with a grammatically broken sentence ('While convert flow matching's determinsitic...'); a broken cross-reference 'Tab. ??' appears in Sec. 4.3; the intro repeats the same sentences about groupwise comparison verbatim; Appendix Section D.1 ('Evaluation on Multi-Subject Scenarios') is an empty heading with no content; Table S.4's columns appear misaligned.

Unexplained and possibly suspicious evidence: the baseline marker '⋆' on the authors' rows in Tables 1-2 is never defined, leaving unclear whether the base model was trained with comparable data/compute to baselines. In Fig. 1, two different prompts yield identical 'Face Score: 0.84' values for Ours, and the teaser compares against Phantom using a real public figure's likeness, which is at odds with the paper's own ethics statement claiming avoidance of real-world public figures.

Some ablation results undermine the central architectural narrative: removing the VLM encoder reduces FaceSim by only 2% (Table 2), and in Table S.5, Stages 1 and 2 of the hierarchical attention contribute little (1-3% FaceSim), suggesting the headline 'hierarchical identity-preserving attention' is mostly stage 3, i.e., a standard cross-attention over concatenated tokens — exactly the baseline it is claimed to beat.

Reproducibility concerns from proprietary dependencies: the data pipeline relies on a closed-source commercial image editor ('Nano Banana'/Gemini-Flash-Image), and the internal 'High-Quality Internal Collection' (9,374 videos) is not described as releasable, so the exact training distribution cannot be reproduced; release of the model/dataset is only promised, not evidenced (no code/project link).

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation: comparisons against strong open-source baselines (Phantom 1.3B/14B, VACE, SkyReels-A2) at matched parameter scales, plus qualitative comparison with proprietary systems (Vidu, Pika, Kling), evaluated on a public benchmark protocol (OpenS2V-Nexus) with a claimed held-out test set.

Thorough ablation coverage: the contribution of each component (hierarchical attention, VLM encoder, curated data, online RL, and individual reward terms, and individual attention stages in Table S.5) is isolated, and the reward-component ablation transparently reveals a reward-hacking trade-off when the naturalness term is removed.

A human preference study (200 questionnaires, 30 participants, four criteria) partially mitigates the circularity of automated metrics and corroborates the quantitative gains, particularly in identity consistency and motion naturalness.

Detailed supplementary material (architecture configuration, GRPO hyperparameters, reward sensitivity analysis, data composition statistics) improves reproducibility, and the authors commit to releasing model and dataset.

The system achieves the best reported total score on the benchmark among open-source models (57.05% for the 14B variant vs. 54.46% for Kling 1.6), with a clear FaceSim advantage (60.71–66.10% vs. ≤55.09% for baselines).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. Each of the three pillars is an existing technique: hierarchical/cascaded attention for multi-subject injection resembles Phantom/CINEMA/Concat-ID, VLM-based guidance is acknowledged as used in CINEMA [6], and the RL stage is a direct application of Flow-GRPO/Dance-GRPO. The claim of 'pioneering online RL for multi-subject video generation' is contradicted by their own citation of Identity-GRPO [33], which applies RL to multi-human identity-preserving video generation.

Metric circularity is a material concern: the RL reward is composed of FaceSim, NexusScore, NaturalScore, and the Aesthetic Score (Eqs. 5–8) — the exact same metrics on which the method is then evaluated in Table 1. Improvements on these metrics after RL (e.g., FaceSim 58.12→66.10) may partly reflect optimization against the benchmark rather than genuine quality gains. The human study helps, but no held-out, non-circular metric (e.g., user ratings on a new prompt set) is reported for the main table.

Some reported gains are small or reversed: after online RL, GmeScore drops (64.06→62.20) and NaturalScore drops (71.09→69.15); the total-score margin over the strongest open-source baseline is modest and no significance analysis is provided. The blanket claim of 'state-of-the-art performance across all evaluation metrics' is overstated.

Contradictory and imprecise statements undermine confidence: (i) NexusScore is described as 'a metric from our proposed OpenS2V-Eval benchmark' when it originates from OpenS2V-Nexus [68]; (ii) the subject image encoder is described as a 'pretrained image encoder' in Sec. 3.2 but as the frozen Wan-Video VAE in the appendix; (iii) the ethics statement claims avoidance of real-world public figures, yet Figure 2 uses a Taylor Swift reference image; (iv) references [66] and [67] are duplicate entries, and the FaceSim metric is attributed to the wrong source.

Presentation quality issues: a broken cross-reference ('As shown in Tab. ??' in Sec. 4.3), a typo in Eq. 3 (Â_{i,ti}), inconsistent notation between Eq. 3 and Eq. S.12, and incomplete GRPO details in the main text (group size G, clip ε, KL coefficient β, rollout steps are not all specified).

The contribution of the curated dataset is entangled with public resources: the dominant data source (218,230 videos from OpenS2V-Nexus) is external, so it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the authors' curation (synthetic compositions, professional videos, ~15k images) versus simply training on the benchmark's own large-scale data. The claimed train/test disjointness is asserted but not verifiable.

Qualitative figures (Figs. 1, 4, 5, 6) are difficult to judge reliably in the manuscript; no quantitative multi-subject-specific evaluation is provided (Sec. D.1 is empty), despite multi-subject composition being the paper's central claim.
